title: David's Charge and Solomon's Kingdom Secured
summary: On his deathbed David charges Solomon to keep the law of Moses so that God's promise to his house will stand, and then he instructs him to deal with Joab and Shimei and to show kindness to Barzillai's sons. After David's death, Adonijah asks for Abishag as his wife, and Solomon, seeing a bid for the throne, has him executed. Solomon banishes the priest Abiathar, has Joab killed at the altar, and later executes Shimei for breaking the terms of his confinement, so that the kingdom is firmly established in his hand.
story: Chapter 1 made Solomon king; chapter 2 makes his kingdom secure. The chapter opens with David's last words to his son, which join the spiritual and the political in a way that troubles many readers. The first half is pure Deuteronomy: be strong, keep God's law, walk in his ways. The second half settles old scores that David himself had left unresolved. Then David dies, after forty years as king, and the narrator repeats a key phrase twice (verses 12 and 46): the kingdom was firmly established. Between those two notes Solomon removes every figure who could threaten him. The promise of 2 Samuel 7, that God would establish the kingdom of David's son, is being kept, but through a series of deaths that leave the reader asking what kind of king Solomon will be.
historical:
David's death is usually dated to about 970 BC. The forty years of his reign (verse 11) are divided as in 2 Samuel 5:4-5, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. The threats Solomon removes had real power bases. Adonijah had support among the royal princes, the army, and part of the priesthood. Joab had commanded the army for most of David's reign. Abiathar was the last survivor of the priestly family of Eli, who had served at Shiloh, and his banishment to Anathoth, a priestly town a few miles northeast of Jerusalem, left Zadok and his descendants as the leading priestly line. The narrator ties this to the prophecy against Eli's house in 1 Samuel 2:27-36. Jeremiah, centuries later, came from a priestly family of Anathoth (Jeremiah 1:1); some scholars think he may have descended from Abiathar, but the text does not say so.

Shimei belonged to Saul's clan and had cursed David as he fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 16:5-13), then begged for mercy on David's return (2 Samuel 19:16-23). He represented the lingering resentment of Saul's supporters in Benjamin. Gath, where his slaves fled, was a Philistine city whose king still had dealings with Israel.
cultural:
Adonijah's request for Abishag was not simply romantic. In the ancient Near East, taking a former king's wives or concubines was a way of claiming his authority; Absalom had done exactly this (2 Samuel 16:21-22), and Abner's relationship with Saul's concubine had been read the same way (2 Samuel 3:7). Abishag had served David intimately, and marrying her would strengthen the claim of the older brother who had already been hailed as king. Solomon reads the request as treason.

The queen mother held a place of honor and influence in Israel and Judah. Solomon rises, bows to Bathsheba, and seats her on a throne at his right hand, the place of highest honor. Later in Kings, the name of each Judean king's mother is recorded, a sign of her public role. Sanctuary at the altar (verses 28-34) had its limits: Exodus 21:14 says a man who kills another deliberately is to be taken even from God's altar. Solomon uses that principle to justify killing Joab in the tent of the LORD. The Kidron Valley ran along the east side of Jerusalem, and crossing it marked leaving the city.
literary: The chapter is framed by David's charge (verses 1-9) and the repeated statement that Solomon's kingdom was firmly established (verses 12 and 46). In between come three episodes, each ending in a death or a banishment: Adonijah (verses 13-25), Abiathar and Joab (verses 26-35), and Shimei (verses 36-46). Each is built on dialogue, and in each the victim's own words or actions provide the legal ground for Solomon's action. David's charge itself is carefully structured: two appeals to faithfulness frame a conditional promise, followed by three instructions on people (Joab, Barzillai's sons, Shimei). The language of wisdom appears in David's instructions (verse 6, “according to your wisdom,” and verse 9, “a wise man”), which is striking because chapter 3 will show God giving Solomon wisdom. Here wisdom seems to mean political shrewdness; there it will mean the discernment to govern justly.

outline.t: David's charge: keep the law of the LORD
Instructions about Joab, Barzillai's sons, and Shimei
David's death and Solomon's established throne

doctrines.note: David's charge ties the future of the dynasty to obedience to the Law of Moses. The language echoes Deuteronomy and Joshua 1, and it sets the standard by which every king in Kings will be judged.

Verse 4 presents God's promise to David as conditional on his descendants' faithfulness, while 2 Samuel 7 stressed that God would never take his steadfast love away. The Bible holds both: an unbreakable promise to the dynasty and real consequences for each king's unfaithfulness.

The narrator presents the deaths of Joab and Shimei as blood coming back upon their own heads, and Abiathar's banishment as fulfilling the word against Eli's house. God's judgment works through history, even through a king's political calculations.

words.note: Kun, to establish or make firm. It appears in verses 12, 24, 45, and 46, echoing God's promise in 2 Samuel 7 to establish David's kingdom and throne. The repetition says that God is keeping his word, while leaving the reader to weigh the means.

Dam, blood, used seven times in this chapter. Blood shed in peacetime stains Joab, his blood will return on his own head, and Shimei's blood will be on his own head. In Israel's thought, innocent blood created guilt that had to be answered, and the chapter uses the word to frame Solomon's actions as justice.

Chokmah, wisdom: skill in living, which can mean practical cleverness, craftsmanship, or moral discernment. David tells Solomon to act according to his wisdom in dealing with Joab. Chapter 3 will show a deeper wisdom given by God, to discern between good and evil in judging his people.

Shamar, to keep, guard, or obey. David tells Solomon to keep the charge of the LORD and his statutes. The same verb runs through Deuteronomy and describes the watchful, careful obedience that the book of Kings will measure every king against.

christ: This chapter shows how a kingdom is established in a world of rivals: by removing them. Solomon's throne is secured, as God promised, but through executions. The New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David whose kingdom is established in a different way. When Peter drew a sword, Jesus told him to put it away (John 18:10-11), and he told Pilate that his kingdom is not of this world, or his servants would fight (John 18:36). Where Solomon's enemies die so that he may reign, Jesus dies for his enemies (Romans 5:10) and then is raised to the throne. David's charge to keep God's law so that the promise may stand also looks forward: no son of David kept it perfectly until the one the New Testament calls obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8). These are contrasts drawn by the later story, not predictions within the chapter.

hard.q: Is Solomon's bloody consolidation of power justice or ruthless politics, and why does David ask for vengeance on his deathbed?
hard.a: Readers are divided, and the text itself gives material for both views. On one reading, each man condemned himself: Joab had murdered Abner and Amasa and backed a rival king, Adonijah's request was an act of treason, and Shimei broke a sworn oath. The narrator frames the deaths in legal terms and ties them to God's justice and to prophecy. On another reading, the chapter quietly exposes the ruthlessness of court politics: David had sworn not to kill Shimei himself and passes the task to his son, and the charges serve Solomon's security neatly. Many interpreters hold both together. The narrator in Kings often reports what kings did without endorsing every act, and the account of Solomon's reign will later turn critical. What is clear is that the throne is established as God promised, and that human motives in the process are mixed.

questions: David's final words mix faithful counsel with unfinished grudges. What unfinished business might you be tempted to hand on to others rather than resolve yourself?
The chapter repeats that the kingdom was firmly established. What makes something truly secure in your life, and what only looks secure?
David asked Solomon to show kindness to Barzillai's sons for their father's loyalty. Whose past faithfulness to you or your family could you honor?
